subtopic.title: Point on an Axis Equidistant from Two Fixed Points

production_run.note: Core1/Core1A/Core1B/Core2 may proceed. Core2A and therefore Core2B must not compile without knowledge percentage or explicit owner waiver.

capabilities.statement: A point on the x-axis has the form P=(x,0).
Squared distance from P=(x,0) to (a,b) is (x-a)^2+b^2.
Equidistant means the two squared distances are equal.
After expansion, the x^2 terms cancel and the remaining equation is linear in x.

concept_boundaries: Averaging x-coordinates is a shortcut only when the geometry supplies the required symmetry; it is not the general method.
The unknown point must be parameterised from the axis constraint before the distance equation is built.

subsubtopics: Build the first right-triangle distance model
Build the second right-triangle distance model
Translate equidistant into equality of squared distances
Expand and see why x^2 cancels
Contrast with a case where averaging x-coordinates fails
Reconstruct the equation from a coordinate diagram
Fade support from guided to independent
Connect the algebraic solution to the perpendicular-bisector locus

must_make_visible: horizontal and vertical offsets to each fixed point
must_not_imply: P is the midpoint of A and B

must_make_visible: each squared distance is horizontal_offset^2 + vertical_offset^2
both distances share the same unknown x
all equidistant points form a perpendicular-bisector locus
the required answer is the intersection with the chosen axis
must_not_imply: the axis itself is always the perpendicular bisector

equation_assimilation.physical_question: Which point P on the x-axis is equally far from A and B?
equation_assimilation.parent_model: distance formula derived from Pythagorean theorem
equation_assimilation.legitimacy: Distances are non-negative, so PA=PB is equivalent to PA^2=PB^2; squaring removes radicals without changing equality.
equation_assimilation.validity_limit: If the reduced coefficient of x is zero, inspect the geometry/equation separately rather than dividing by zero.

blocks.prompt: For A(1,2), B(5,2), P on the x-axis, compare symmetry with the general squared-distance method.
For A(-1,4), B(7,2), test the claim that averaging x-coordinates always gives the answer.
For A(-2,3), B(4,1), fill the missing coordinate model, squared distances, and final linear step.
For A(0,5), B(6,1), solve with only P=(x,0) supplied.
Change only the axis or the fixed-point height relation and predict whether the shortcut remains valid.
A(-4,3), B(2,1); P lies on the y-axis and is equidistant from A and B. Find P.

core2.anchor_problem: Find the point P on the x-axis that is equidistant from A(-1,4) and B(7,2).
core2.recognition_cue: x-axis constraint plus equal distances to two fixed points
core2.hidden_state_or_event: The unknown is a constrained point P=(x,0), not an unconstrained pair (x,y).
core2.first_non_obvious_move: Parameterise the point as P=(x,0) before writing any distance expression.
core2.representation_switch: word/coordinate description -> two squared-distance expressions -> linear equation
core2.common_wrong_chain: Average -1 and 7 to get x=3 without checking the unequal y-coordinates.
core2.check: Substitute x=9/4 into both squared distances and confirm equality.
